entry.title: AI Music Platform, Designed to Get Out of the Way
entry.summary: Designing Beatoven.ai: an intuitive AI music generator for custom background music Role:…
entry.content:
Designing Beatoven.ai: an intuitive AI music generator for custom background music

Role: Lead Designer (Brand, Web & Product Design, Art Direction)

Problem

 

Background music plays a crucial role in elevating content. It must match the mood, theme, and vibe: stock music rarely works. Custom music creation was expensive and accessible only to large production houses.
Creators, marketers, and indie filmmakers wanted custom, royalty-free background music that matched their content's mood, but lacked the resources and technical knowledge to compose it. They also couldn't afford to hire music composers.
Beatoven.ai had created a powerful AI engine capable of generating original, mood-based music. But they needed a clear visual identity, intuitive product experience, and scalable design system to reach a larger audience, make the product popular, and attract investors.
 

Approach

 
As Lead Designer, I defined and executed every visual and experiential aspect of Beatoven.ai — from brand identity and website to product interfaces and marketing presence.
 
I began by interviewing users to understand their challenges and studying competitor products for insights. I defined a unified brand direction—vibrant, creative, and tech-forward—that celebrated music creation as an emotional, intuitive experience. I then established guidelines for the website and both web and mobile products, building a framework for an intuitive workflow familiar to our users. Throughout product development, we iterated extensively on features. Some stayed, others were removed to strengthen the product.

Research & Insights

 
We interviewed 150+ creators — musicians, YouTube creators, filmmakers, and content creators — and discovered key insights:
  1. Users struggled to search for the music they wanted. They wished they could hum it or explain it as they would to a music composer.
  2. Finding music that matched the mood they were looking for took days. Even when they found something, it rarely matched the length they needed.
  3. Content creators constantly faced copyright strikes.
  4. Royalty-free music lacked the quality filmmakers needed.
  5. They primarily worked with professional tools like Adobe Premiere and DaVinci Resolve, which became the inspiration for the product's visual and interaction style.
  6. Music creation needed emotional depth, not just automation. Users wanted to feel in control — they preferred mood-driven inputs like "uplifting," "dreamy," or "intense" rather than technical ones.
  7. The brand needed to feel creative yet credible. Our audience ranged from indie YouTubers to ad agencies — visuals had to balance fun and professionalism.

Solution

 

I designed a cohesive design ecosystem that powered the brand, website, and product experience. I simplified the product workflow so that even a child could use it to create music. I iterated on features, studied usage patterns, and solidified the core functionality.
 
 

1. Product Design (Web & Mobile)

 
(Key features that stayed: text-based prompting to define music preferences, reference tracks, editing controls, create similar, sharing, extend and shorten, music licenses, plugin exploration, and track history, adding video to match music, themes, collaboration, and various editing options.)
Beatoven's product was designed to make AI music creation intuitive and joyful. From the Workspace to track editing screens, the interface guided users through creation with minimal friction.
 
Understanding the Existing Workflow Before redesigning, I studied how creators sourced background music. Most relied on royalty-free websites — searching with vague keywords, spending hours filtering, and rarely finding the perfect fit. Once they found a track, their workflow in video editors worked well, as they could trim, loop, and sync it easily. Their process followed three broad steps: 1. Search & Describe: Find music through keyword-based searches. 2. Explore & Select: Compare options and save potential matches. 3. Customize & Sync: Manually edit and sync tracks in video editors. The workflow was familiar but fragmented — finding, licensing, and organizing music was slow and interrupted creative flow.
 
After — Redesigning the Experience
Instead of reinventing the process, I refined it — keeping the familiar flow but removing friction and adding intelligence. The redesigned workflow became: 1. Create Track: Describe the mood or upload a reference audio or video — no keywords needed. 2. Explore & Iterate: Instantly review and refine AI-generated tracks, saving favorites. 3. Edit Track: Adjust energy, duration, and structure directly in the workspace. 4. Share & Export: Share with collaborators and export ready-to-use, licensed tracks. This new flow preserved what users already knew while solving their biggest pain points — finding the right music, managing licenses, and staying in creative flow.
 
 
 
 

 

2. Brand & Visual Language

 

Moodboard

 

The visual identity reflected creativity and technology — gradients inspired by sound waves, clean typography, and expressive motion. I chose a dark mode so that neon and bright colors could pop. The product was simple and intuitive, while social media and the website were energetic and vibrant.
I built a reference style guide and design system that could scale across multiple products — including the main app, landing pages, and marketing campaigns.
 
 

UI component library

 

 

3. Web Experience

 

The marketing website was designed to reflect the product’s clarity and creativity — but with added vibrancy and energy. Each section highlighted how simple it was to create original music while keeping the brand’s playful and approachable tone. We also spotlighted artist contributions to reinforce Beatoven.ai’s position as one of the few ethical AI music companies. I proposed a hands-on approach where users could start creating a track right from the homepage, allowing them to experience the product’s capability firsthand.
 

4. Merchandise & Brand Collateral

 

To strengthen the identity, I extended the visual language into merchandise and social media — ensuring every touchpoint felt consistent and expressive. The t-shirts were a big hit! Musicians and students kept asking for more. Beatoven became a popular name in the community.
 
 
 
 
I also set motion and video guidelines for brand films, defining rhythm, typography movement, and visual pacing.
 
 

Outcome

 

Beatoven.ai launched with a bold identity and user-friendly product that resonated with creators and professionals alike. The platform saw significant growth in engagement, and the brand became synonymous with AI music that feels human.
 

My Learning

 

A scalable design system builds creative freedom, not restriction.
Music interfaces must translate emotion into usability — minimal friction, maximum delight. Aligning brand, product, and marketing under one unified design language creates a strong, memorable impression.

entry.title: Travel Management Platform, Designed to Be Enjoyed
entry.summary: Insteract simplifies travel management by blending traveller needs and company policies. It…
entry.content:
Insteract simplifies travel management by blending traveller needs and company policies. It offers a complete travel management platform for business and travellers.

Role: UX/UI design, Visual design, Prototyping

Problem

Business travel is essential for geographically distributed teams, but managing it was hard work.

Travellers were unhappy with the bookings made by agents.

Travellers spent a lot of time coordinating with the travel team to get the flights they wanted. In most cases, the team was not aware of their personal preferences and could not book flights that they liked.

Travel managers struggled to define the best travel policy.

Travel managers spent a lot of time getting the best flights and rates from agents. They struggled to define the best travel policy that worked well for both the company and the employees.

Solution

 

We built a complete travel platform to simplify travel management.

1) Travellers got a dependable, personalised travel assistant.

The mobile app understood the traveller's personal preferences and blended them with the travel policy to always show relevant results. They could book flights that they liked while staying within the budget.

2) Travel managers got control over the workflow

The mobile and the web app allowed them to get control over the workflow from anywhere.

Onboarding Travellers

 

Collecting traveller preferences upfront helped us show relevant results.

Travellers were very picky about their travel preferences

We got to know the travellers very well. Their likes, dislikes and travel preferences. We were not pesky, the short questions were easy to answer with a few taps. This helped us personalise the experience and always show relevant content.

 

Flight Search

 

Business travellers did not want to spend time looking for the cheapest flights.

Show the best personalised results

We found that travellers spent too much time looking for the flights that matched their preferences and the company policies. We only showed flights that matched the company policy.

Shortcuts for frequent destination

Travellers frequently took flights to the same destination. We created shortcuts to frequent locations to make it easy.

Allow designated employees to book trips

Sometimes a designated employee would book tickets for travellers, we allowed these employees to book tickets for multiple travellers.

Flight Results

 

Travellers did not want endless choices, only relevant choices.

Show compact, easy to compare results

We picked the most important information that could help make quick decisions.

Show layover times

The cheapest flights had the most number of connections and the longest layover times. We showed the amenities and layover time upfront.

Show validation for the recommendation

We should the exact reasons for a recommendation. This helped travellers make a calculated decision.

Self Booking

 

Travellers liked the freedom of booking their flights.

Save card information

We found that travellers preferred to use the same cards to book their flights. we saved the information for commonly used cards to help book faster.

Other was to pay

The travellers would occasionally use other methods to pay. We allowed them to pay using the most common ways.

Manage approvals

 

Travel managers got control over the workflow

Show travel request summary

Managers could see a list of requests. Each request had just enough summary needed to approve a request. Left swipe to approve and right swipe to reject.

Review request details

Some requests needed detailed review. We allowed them to review the details and highlight important information like the policy compliance and the budget upfront.

Outcome

 

The travel management platform helped everybody in the company

Travellers liked the freedom of booking their own travel. Overall they found the experience positive and glad that they did not have to haggle with the travel agents any more.

Travel managers could concentrate on designing better travel policies. They did not spend any time coordinating with the travellers and agents.

Learning

 

It is important to keep everybody on the team up-to-date on the design details.

The final product will look as good as the documentation. Designers need to document the execution details because not everything is obvious in the Sketch or Figma file.

Mockup every screen for every flow to make everything crystal clear. This may seem like a daunting task, but it will be helpful during execution.

Add annotations and explanation to the design file. This will document all the design decisions. This will come in handy when you have to defend the design decisions.

Visually explain all the animations and transitions needed to take the experience to the next level. Use Framer or Principal to create prototypes for the animations. They help get a faster buy-in from the team.

entry.title: Nymble: A Robotic Cooking Assistant, Your Personal Chef
entry.summary: Nymble had a unique idea to automate boring parts of cooking so…
entry.content:
Nymble had a unique idea to automate boring parts of cooking so people could enjoy what they really loved- Eating!

Role: UX/UI design, Visual design, Prototyping

Problem

We were just a few months away from CES, the most influential tech event in the world. Nymble wanted to show their product fondly called "Julia" to potential customers, investors and tech enthusiasts. Julia could cook a variety of meals, but had difficulty communicating with humans.

Approach

I started out by understanding the current "smart cooker" space. I found that there were 2 types of interfaces – 1) A small digital screen with buttons to interact with the appliance and 2) A full-screen display with one or no buttons.

Next, I understood the design of the appliance itself – It would be a modern, minimalistic appliance with very few buttons. It would have smooth contours and no hard edges.

Finally, I understood how the device would be used – It would be used mostly in the kitchen under different lighting conditions. People would use it standing about 1 foot away from it.

Insights

1) The interface had to be dark to emit very less light from the screen. It would be used both in the night and day.

2) The interface had to be fully screen-based to match the aesthetics of the appliance.

3) The text and images had to be legible from a distance.

Inspiration

I drew inspiration from other smart devices that had a full digital display and controls.

Starry Router – Touchscreen router.
June – Smart Oven

Solution

I build a click-through prototype that simulated all the features of Julia.

Julia could show recipes from all over the world. The prototype guided users to choose a recipe, prepare ingredients and see the progress. It also prompted them to complete an action when needed.

Mood board showing the appliance aesthetics and style for the icons, UI, Fonts and Images.

Navigation

The navigation system was designed to be simple so users could concentrate on the task at hand.

We identified 4 things the device UI had to support:

1) Show a restaurant style menu

We found that people bored of the same food, that's why they like to try new things often. Julia could show a regularly changing menu to keep the interest going.

2) Show cooking time and ingredients

Peopled picked a dish based on the amount of time they had and the ingredients available. It was important to show the ingredients and cooking time to help them make a decision.

3) Show ingredient preparation

Some dishes had to be prepared manually. Users needed to know how to prepare the ingredients without moving away from the recipe. We showed preparation videos as part of the recipe to allow them to follow along.

4) Prompt user when needed

Some recipes needed users to complete a task before moving forward. We prompted users to complete the task. Example: Flipping over a steak.

Navigation Flow for cooking a steak with Julia

Restaurant style menu

 
We found that people get bored of the same food, that's why they like to try new things often. Julia could show a regularly changing menu to keep the interest going.

Our research showed that people liked to eat quick meals when they were in a hurry but, enjoyed cooking alone or with friends and family as a pass time. Julia had 2 modes for this – Auto and Guided

Most people ate meals based on what they felt like eating. Instead of Breakfast, lunch or dinner, they would like to eat a light snack a dessert or a filling meal.

Visual Ingredients

Peopled picked a dish based on the amount of time they had and the ingredients available. It was important to show the ingredients and cooking time to help them make a decision.

We borrowed the photography style from real restaurant menus. We used mouthwatering photos of the dish and ingredients to build up an appetite.

Prepare ingredients

Some dishes had to be prepared manually. Users needed to know how to prepare the ingredients without moving away from the recipe. We showed preparation videos as part of the recipe to help them to follow along.

Most of our users already cooked while watching recipe videos. We used the same idea to create mini videos with captions to help users easily follow along.

Prompt users

Some recipes needed users to complete a task before moving forward. We prompted users to complete the task.

Users could be away from the appliance, so we used sounds as well to call for attention.

We used animation to show actions – Weighing scale showed the actual weight and the arrow indicated a flip action.

Outcome

 
The product demo was a hit! The physical device and the UI worked very well and showed the full experience to thousands of visitors.

The team was able to get some interest from high profile investors, hardware manufacturers and technology enthusiasts.

They also collect emails of interested visitors which could later be used for marketing and user testing.

My Learning

This was my first project for a physical device. Designing for a physical device is very different from designing for the mobile and web. A few things I learnt on the way:

1) Consider the distance between the interface and the user earlier on. Account for the distance to design the best size for the fonts, graphics and buttons.

2) The graphic capability of the display can be limiting. Use this as a constraint for designing minimal graphics and better text.

3) The display will usually interact with physical buttons on the device. Make sure the placement of the buttons are intuitive

4) Devices also use sounds, vibration and lights to communicate with users. knowledge of these will help in designing a better experience.

entry.title: Emtropy: AI-Powered Feedback Analysis, Gamified for Everyday Use
entry.summary: People spend the majority of their day at work. It's important to…
entry.content:
People spend the majority of their day at work. It's important to build a culture of open feedback, appreciation and continuous learning for everybody to thrive.

Role: User Research, UX/UI design, Visual design, Prototyping

Problem

Employee performance systems are broken. Appraisals alone can't help individuals become better. These are good for evaluation but fail to improve performance. Both appraisers and appraisers dislike the long, laborious process. We set out to change this system by designing a performance-focused solution.

Research

We spoke to 30+ people across different roles and company sizes. Small startups to large corporations. Individual contributors to Directors. It was clear, everybody felt that regular feedback was essential for progress.

Our research showed that employees needed a transparent feedback system that was less formal and more frequent. They needed feedback in context to what they were doing, not after it was done.

Key insights:

Frequent, context based 2-way feedback

The usual appraisal feedback is one way and does not help in identifying areas for improvement. The appraisal process is long and tedious and assesses work done in the past.

Employees found that getting feedback in context to their current work helped them do better. Any contextual feedback was offline and was not recorded. So, it was forgotten during the appraisal interviews.

Appreciating small wins in public built reciprocity

Everybody feels good when they are appreciated for their efforts. We assumed that appreciation had to be private and personal.

We learnt that in addition to this, most people liked it when they are appreciating it in public. We also found that It is easier to reciprocate and show appreciation in return.

Self paced and hands-on learning

Traditional learning programs are designed to align employees with the company needs. Employees completed these programs but it did not contribute to their progress.

We found that employees have to be continuously coached on new things. Learning depended on applying their knowledge in everyday work for a considerable amount of time.

Solution

 

Armed with these insights, we set out to design a solution that integrated Feedback, Appreciation and Learning into one cohesive solution.

Feedback

We found 2 things that were causing problems exchanging feedback freely.

1) There was initial hesitation to give and receive feedback.

We found that Managers were comfortable giving feedback to their team. But, the team members were wary of requesting feedback even though they knew it was important .

We helped start the habit by nudging them to take action.

2) Feedback was perceived as harsh or negative

Giving and receiving feedback was tough. Well-intended feedback could sound rude and demotivate the receiver if not given the right way.

We designed the process of giving feedback into 2 sections - Positive feedback first, followed by ways to improve. This made sure that the feedback was well rounded and motivating.

 

Kudos

We found that appreciating each other was contagious. The more employees liked each other, the better they felt.

1) Share wins with the world

Earlier wins were celebrated, but offline. The value of the appreciation multiplied when everybody could participate in the celebration.

We made sharing wins easy. Just one tap to share appreciation on social media.

 

2) Reciprocate appreciation

We found that appreciation created natural reciprocation. People who appreciate their teammates and managers got appreciated in return. As a result, teams bonded well and indirectly helped their productivity and performance.

It was easy to like, share and respond to appreciation messages when they were shown in a public feed.

 

3) Strengthen company culture

Most companies struggle to build a culture. Culture is built on shared company values. Even with the most amount of efforts from HR teams, not everybody really knows and behaves in accordance with the company culture.

We helped people remember the values and act accordingly by the act of repetition. Every appreciation was linked to company values.

Learning

We discovered that for learning to be effective, it had to be self paced and hands on.

1) Self Paced learning

Employees learn better when they learn what they wanted at their own pace. But, it's difficult for them to complete the program if they are left to learn on there own.

To solve this problem, we nudged employees to complete the programs by showing their progress in the dashboard.

 

2) Hands on learning

Employees had to apply learning in everyday work to make real progress. There was no way to see if there was progress even if they got to apply their learning.

We analysed the skills for each feedback message. This helped us show progress over time.

Outcome

Users loved the way we integrated feedback, appreciation and learning.

We solved a gap in the current HR systems by creating a platform for employees to exchange feedback openly, appreciate teammates and be appreciated in return. They learnt skills that they needed the most at their own pace and applied it in their everyday work.

My Learning

 

I learnt many important lessons during the course of the design.

Get as much real data as possible

Most times decisions are made based on what the feels, not really how the users feel. To make objective decisions it is important to get real data.

Learn from cross-functional teams

Product Managers and Developers have the same goal as designers but, a completely different way of thinking. Getting reviews from a cross-functional team opens up new doors.
